Doing a Burl
Justice
by Keith Ruttan
I acquired a large Maple burl at our Guild wood raffle recently
which was won by George Wood. It measured roughly 18” x 15”
x 5”. He donated it to me and said “I’ll give you this as you will
do it justice—thank you for all your help over the years”.
The idea for the piece came from my son Eric who showed
me a photo of this type of bowl he had seen on the Internet.
It took some planning to figure out how to balance it on the
lathe and keep it all in one piece—some of it when I couldn’t
sleep at 3 am!
I created a sacrifi
cial tenon so that I could
grip the bottom of the
piece to avoid using a
faceplate on the bot
tom (and therefore no
screw holes). I carefully
positioned the sacrifi
cial piece so I could turn
it on the lathe. Next I
made a mortise on the
top of the bowl so that once flipped over, I could finish off the
bottom by removing the sacrificial piece of wood and make
a new mortise complete with my signature bead & button
details.
With the bottom sanded, I began the process of turning the
outside edge of the
form. Turning the flat
surface was a challenge
and I made a scraper to
carefully clean out the
remaining wood on the
base of the bowl where
it meets the platter.
Finally, I carefully hol
lowed-out the inside of
the bowl.
Onto finishing... On the
platter face I scribbled a pencil guideline so that I could evenly
sand with an orbital sander by just removing the lines careful
ly, with each grit of sandpaper, then hand sanded where the
orbital sander couldn’t reach.
For the inside of the bowl I had to do a lot of hand sanding
because of the live edge of the burl. It was sanded to 320 grit
and finished with 5-8 coats of wipe-on Polyurethane.
Got a project you’d like to see featured in our front page?
Get in touch by email: editor@gvwg.ca

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | J U N E 2 0 2 6
President’s Message
by Don Gamble
Over the past while, I’ve been looking at woodturning
communities in New Zealand, and something kept catching
my attention. In places like Auckland and Rotorua, their
guilds don’t just meet once a month - they meet multiple
times a week. Members gather in shared workshop spaces
to turn, learn, experiment, and simply spend time together.
It’s a rhythm that feels very different from what we’re used
to here, more continuous and more social, almost as if the
workshop is a natural extension of everyday life.
When I mentioned this to Pippa Lattey, she said the same
thing happens in Australia. We both wondered whether this
model grew out of, or was at least influenced by the “Men’s
Shed” movement that’s so common down there. Despite the
name, Men’s Sheds aren’t necessarily men‑only, and many
have evolved into mixed‑gender or community‑wide spaces.
The name is more historical than anything. What matters is
the spirit: a workshop as a social hub, a place where people
drop in, work on projects, share skills, and build friendships
in a natural, unstructured way.
There are a few examples of similar spaces in Canada, but
nothing on the scale or with the cultural presence you see in
New Zealand and Australia. Here, the idea exists in pockets
- community centers, maker spaces, volunteer shops - but it
hasn’t become a widespread model.
All of this made me think about our own Guild. We actual
ly have access to a shared workshop: the KMS Workshop
space. It’s well-equipped with multiple lathes, sharpening,
tools, and everything needed for hands-on turning. It’s not
well-organized, or at least not yet, but with a bit of elbow
grease it certainly could be. Right now though, we use it al
most exclusively for structured classes. People arrive, learn,
clean up, and head home. It works beautifully for teaching,
but it’s a very different model from the open, drop‑in, com
munity‑shop approach that seems to thrive elsewhere.
So I found myself wondering what it would look like if we
imagined something more. Not a plan, not a proposal - just
a bit of dreaming based on what already exists.
What if the KMS Workshop space were part of the Guild’s
weekly rhythm? What if members could come in to practice
a cut, try a new tool, or work on a project alongside others?
What if experienced turners could mentor informally, and
newer turners could build confidence through repetition
rather than waiting for the next class? What if small dem
os happened because someone was experimenting with
texturing or spindle work and others gathered around to
watch? What if the Guild’s sense of community wasn’t tied to
a calendar date, but to a shared space?
It’s interesting to imagine how that kind of environment
might shape our culture. Right now, the Guild’s energy
comes from a few highly involved volunteers who make our
events and classes possible. A more open workshop model
would shift that dynamic. Instead of relying on a small core,
the community itself becomes the engine - people showing
up, helping each other, sharing knowledge, and building
momentum simply by being present.
Of course, dreaming is the easy part. The practical side is
more complicated. Space, insurance, supervision, funding,
volunteer capacity - all of these would need careful thought.
And in our case, there’s an additional consideration: the KMS
Workshop space belongs to KMS Tools. We use it with their
blessing for classes, but expanding that into a more open,
drop‑in model would require their support and partnership.
That’s not a small detail; it’s a foundational one.
And it raises a question: would it make sense to call this idea
a “Men’s/Women’s Shed spirit”? Maybe. The name isn’t the
important part. What matters is the idea of a shared space
where turning, learning, and connection happen naturally
and continuously. Maybe this kind of model doesn’t fit our
membership, or our geography, or our realities. But some
times it’s worth letting ourselves imagine what the next
chapter could look like, even if it never becomes more than
a conversation.
So this month, I’m simply sharing the question that’s been
on my mind: if we could shape a space that supports turn
ing, learning, and community in a more continuous way—
something with a little of that Men’s/Women’s Shed spirit,
what might it look like for GVWG?
No decisions. No direction. Just a bit of dreaming.
—Don Gamble

Editor’s Notes
by Britchie
Greetings fellow woodturners.
Most of my effort on the newsletter for the first couple of
issues has gone into the visual design, flow and production
streamlining etc. But I’ve also been working in the back
ground on some new content initiatives.
One of the results of this effort is a new piece written by Mike
Moult called “Know your Species”. As the title suggests it’s all
about trees and wood in relation to our discipline—the kind
of stuff we should all be a little more familiar with (speaking
for myself of course!). The article covers identification, com
mon uses, turning value, hardness, cultural and historical
significance. Mike has agreed to enlighten us all with a dif
ferent species each month. I’ve some plans for some other
monthly features but let me know what you think to this.
Our cover this month features a superb bowl/platter by
Keith Ruttan. As soon as I saw the photo of him holding
this unique piece, I knew this was going to be our next front
page. I’m grateful to Keith (and his wife Jean) for indulging
me and for pushing through the challenges of writing to
share the story of how this piece came to be.
This month’s member article “Transferring images onto
Wood” has been put together by Marco Berera who details
an interesting option for embellishing wood turnings and
includes a 7-step process for achieving professional results.
After an absence of a couple of months, we have a member
spotlight featuring newcomer Blair Flink and we’ve some
photos and a write-up by Ed Pretty for the “Intro to Spindle
Turning Class” which took place back in May.
And finally, our Instant and President’s Challenge galleries
feature a wealth of member work this month with a total of 7
pages, 4 of them with lidded boxes. I don’t recall a challenge
as well subscribed as this and I’m looking forward to a little
down-time to make some of my own.
Have a Great Summer!

15% Discount for GVWG Members
If you give the cashier your phone number, you will only get
the store 5% non-Guild discount. By saying GVWG instead you
get the 15% Guild discount.
If you are buying something that needs a warranty, just give
them your Name and Address and that will go on the electron
ic file. If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is better
than the 15%, then you will automatically get the better rate.
Every purchase you make in the store by using this process
adds to our GVWG Credit account which we use to buy KMS
gift certificate prizes. We even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this! By doing this you are giving yourself
a better discount and helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out-of-town Guild member, all you have to do is
type in GVWG as the customer name when buying, and type in
your full name, address etc. in the ‘ship-to’ field and you will
get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the cost mar
gins from that manufacturer. This does not apply to published
special flyer items. If we all do this, we can even get up to a
bigger discount level in future!

KMS Classroom Lathes Fixed
by Brian Lunt
Bob Gadd from Woodworker Specialties helped us detail
the noise issues with the belt driven Nova lathe in the KMS
classroom.
We first changed the motor bearings with the expertise from
Steve Daechsel, but the lathe still had some noise. Bob used
a trick that diagnosed the issue. By moving the drive belt
to the largest diameter, the noise stopped. Buy moving the
belt back over to the smaller pully diameter, the noise came
back. This showed the pully was worn on its motor spindle
mounting. So we replaced the pully and the noise went
away.
The next lathe to be fixed was
the 220v DVR XP lathe. This
lathe experienced a pro
longed state of the spindle in
its locked position with the
forward button engaged—all
the while the classroom was
focused on the next step from
the instructor in the bowl
turning class. It was some
thing any one of us could
have done. Smoke was observed coming from the lathe so it
was quickly disconnected.
The first step in diagnosing what needed fixing was to
check all three motor windings. Nova states we should have
between 9 to 11 ohms on each winding. Bob Gilson and I
measured 9.2 ohms so
that was a good sign.
Next was checking for
a short. We used the
continuity setting on
our meter and ground
ed one pin onto bare
metal housing and the
other pin on all six mo
tor power pins. No sound from the meter, which is a good
thing that confirmed the windings were not shorted out.
This moved the focus to the motherboard. After removing
the board and tearing it down to look for char points that
would indicate where the “magic smoke” was let out. None
was found, so this indicated the board had a deeper prob
lem.
Steve Hansen and I
replaced the mother
board with a new one,
re-installed and ran
the lathe through its
paces from 50 RPM to
3,000 RPM, forward and
reverse.
The last maintenance
detail we undertook
was to tighten all the spindle lock bolts (one was really
loose) and vacuum and use compressed air to clean all
the motors. The photo (left) shows how much sawdust we
found.
All worked so we are now back to 7 operating lathes in the
KMS classroom! Thank you to everyone that helped.

Required Materials
•
A smooth sanded wood surface (220–320 grit)
•
A Laser-printed image (IMPORTANT: inkjet prints
usually won’t transfer properly)
•

•

•

•
Water and sponge
•
Fine sandpaper (320–400 grit)
•
Protective topcoat
Tips for Best Results
•
Practice first on a piece of scrap wood.
•
Avoid excessive rubbing, which can remove image
detail (use markers to fix small missing details).
•
For curved spindle work, smaller images or tiled
designs work better than full photos.
•
Multiple thin topcoats produce a smoother, profes
sional finish.

Transferring
Images onto Wood
by Marco Berera
We often like to embellish our woodturnings
with dyes or stains, paint, coloured pencils etc.
How about a printed graphic? Images can be
faithfully transferred onto a flat dish, vessel,
or spindle work while preserving the natural
beauty of the wood. Achieving this depends on
the size of the image and the curvature of the
surface. A common issue is getting the paper
to adhere to the turning. The solution: a ‘wet’
method can be used to successfully to transfer
small tiled images using a water-based polyure
thane.
Prepare the Wood Surface
The wood must be sanded
completely smooth and be
dust-free. Uneven grain or
rough spots can distort the
transfer and should be avoid
ed. Light coloured, low-figure
woods such as Maple, Birch,
or Ash are the most suitable.

M E M B E R A R T I C L E

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | J U N E 2 0 2 6
Apply Polyurethane
Brush a medium coat of
water-based polyurethane
directly onto the wood sur
face where the image will be
placed.
Produce your Image
Print your image at full size
using a laser printer. If your
image has any text in it or
elements that need to orient
correctly, you must flip your
image in reverse in your
graphics software before
printing off.
Position the Image
Carefully place the image
printed side down onto the
wood. Smooth out bubbles
immediately using a credit
card. Since lathe work is
often curved, small images
transfer better on rounded
surfaces than large, complex
ones.
3
2
4
Allow the Image to Dry
Allow the piece to dry thor
oughly for 1 to 2 hours (it
worked for me).
5
Remove the Paper Backing
Dampen the paper with wa
ter, then gently rub away the
paper fibers very gently with
your fingers or a sponge. The
image remains embedded in
the polyurethane layer.
6
Seal the Transfer
After drying, apply additional
coats of water-based polyure
thane to protect the image
and blend it into the wood
finish.

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | J U N E 2 0 2 6
YOUR PERSONAL SAFETY
Always wear Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) such as
approved safety glasses or goggles that include side protec
tors. Use a full face shield for larger bowl, vessel, or any turning
involving chucks and faceplates. Wear a dust mask or an air
filtration helmet in conjunction with proper ventilation and/
or a dust collection system as appropriate. Remember—it’s
the fine airborne particles that are harmful to your respiratory
system. Wear hearing protection during extended periods of
turning.
Tie back long hair and avoid long sleeves or loose clothing.
Remove rings and other jewelry, or any dangling objects that
may catch on rotating parts or accessories.
Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close attention to
unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the
cause. Don’t operate machines when you are tired or under
the influence of drugs or alcohol.
WORKING SAFELY WITH YOUR LATHE
Ensure your workpiece is securely fastened. When using a
faceplate, be certain the workpiece is solidly mounted with
stout screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws as a minimum).
Do not use drywall or deck screws. When turning between
centers, check the workpiece is firmly mounted between the
headstock and tailstock and rotate your workpiece forwards/
backwards by hand to make sure it clears the toolrest and bed
before turning the lathe on.
Check all locking devices on the tailstock and tool rest as
sembly (rest and base) are tight before operating the lathe.
Check the speed of your lathe BEFORE turning it on. Use
slower speeds for larger diameters or rough pieces and higher
speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced.
Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is
balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the speed.
If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the machine to under
stand why. As a starting point, consult your operator’s manual
for recommended speeds for a particular lathe. Ensure the
lathe speed is compatible with the diameter of the blank.
Stay clear of danger zones directly behind and in front of the
workpiece. They are the most likely areas for a piece to travel
as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of
this zone when turning on the lathe, keeping your hand on the
switch in case you need to turn the machine off. When observ
ing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
Turn the lathe off before adjusting anything including the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches, and knock
out bars immediately after use. Never leave them in place,
even for a moment. Always remove the tool rest before sand
ing, finishing, or polishing operations.
Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced
woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and proce
dures not recommended for beginning turners.
Exercise extra caution when using stock with cracks, splits,
checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular shapes or protuberanc
es. Beginners should avoid these types of stock until they have
greater knowledge of working such wood.
Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding the tool
in a controlled but comfortable manner. Always contact the
tool rest with the tool before contacting the wood.
Never work with a lathe in reverse unless the chuck is using
a locking set-screw. It is possible for a chuck or faceplate to
unscrew unless it is fitted securely on the lathe spindle.
Don’t overreach. Keep proper footing and keep your balance

S A F E T Y G U I D E L I N E S
(Continues on the next page)
You mostly work on your own so safety is
YOUR responsibility. Please take the time to
read our safety guidelines and make them part
of your daily turning practice. Be safe out there!

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | J U N E 2 0 2 6
at all times.
Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer performance.
Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose for which
it was not designed or intended.
Consider your work environment. Don’t use a lathe in damp
or wet locations. Do not use in presence of flammable liquids
or gases, and always keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher
close at hand. Keep your work area well lit.
Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric cords for dam
age. Avoid the use of extension cords.
Never leave a lathe running unattended. Turn power off.
Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
SAFETY MAINTENANCE
Keep your lathe in good repair. Ensure belt guards or protec
tive covers are in place. Check for damaged parts, alignment,
binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect
its operation.
Read and follow safety guidelines for your lathe and other
workshop equipment. Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially bandsaws and chainsaws.

M E M B E R S P O T L I G H T
What’s your background, how did you get into turning?
Back in the Spring of 2020 during Covid lock down, I saw a
video of someone making a bowl on a lathe and got inspired. I
wanted to get into wood working as I had made some fur
niture in high school, but I didn’t have the space for all the
equipment. The lathe seemed like the answer since it’s a
standalone machine that produces finished products and I
had space for one. My wife agreed so I took the plunge. It turns
out that lathes are ‘gateway tools’ that lead people into buying
more and more tools! I have since purchased a 14” bandsaw,
a portable table saw, two chainsaws, a grinder for sharpening
chisels, a 2-stage dust collector, an air purifier, a portable sand
er and a portable planer. Oops!
Tell us about your workshop
I work out of the front part of my two-car garage (which has
never seen a car in it). I have all the equipment listed above
and a couple worktables. I’m working on making everything
mobile with casters, and I’m always trying to improve the
layout and efficiency.
What tools do you like using at your lathe?
I’m fortunate to have quite a few chisels of various types and I
use most of them regularly. My favourite is my bowl gouge and
there are times when I love my carbide-tip chisels too.
Blair Flink
with Diana Dougherty
LEVEL
LOCATION
interests
Langley
Intermediate (100+ pieces made)
Enjoying a rewarding hobby

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | J U N E 2 0 2 6
What finishes do you prefer?
Tung oil and Danish oil finishes are favourites of mine and
sometimes I just apply a beeswax paste.
What is your favourite wood?
I’d have to say that Cherry is my favourite so far. I’ve had great
success with it and love how it looks when finished. I have
made some beautiful pieces from a slab of spalted Maple burl
and I really like the look of Western Red Cedar although it
needs lots of sanding due to tear-out. I haven’t tried that many
varieties of wood and look forward to trying new ones.
Have you incorporated any other materials in your pieces?
I have done quite a few pieces with epoxy additions that are
coloured with mica powder dyes. I made a pencil holder using
pencil crayons and clear epoxy, and tried a piece of Parallam
with epoxy (too many voids to work well). I stitched a crack on
green wood with copper wire and that turned out well (it’s not
a mistake, it’s a FEATURE!).
What other types of woodworking or pursuits do you have?
I built a coffee table and nightstand from red oak back in high
school and am currently building some workshop benches
for portable equipment to make them mobile. I’d like to make
some charcuterie boards using my planer.
What inspires you - where do you get your ideas from?
Until recently, my only influences were from various YouTube
turners. Andy Phillip is one person who comes to mind. I like
unusual creations and shapes and am drawn to trying new
things. Sometimes I just study a piece of wood and a shape or
idea occurs to me. Other times, I know I want to make a certain
size bowl or box and go looking for suitable wood to use.
Who has been the greatest influence on your work?
I don’t think I’ve observed enough of anyone’s work to feel in
fluenced by them. Again, maybe a YouTube channel like Andy
Phillips has influence to some extent.
What is the most challenging piece you have made so far?
I made a flower vase from a fruit tree root ball which was
challenging but turned out quite well. I had difficulty because
of the irregular shape and needed to use caution with the
roots spinning so fast they couldn’t be seen—just felt with my
knuckles. I’m sure others have had similar experiences.
Where do you usually display and/or sell you work?
So far, I have been gifting my pieces to family and friends and
building a sizable collection at home that I need to start sell
ing. I plan to get a booth at various craft fairs and I hope to sell
pieces through my Instagram account @FlinkWoodDesigns.
Feel free to follow me!
What is your favorite project to date?
It’s hard to pick just one. The vase I mentioned is one and a
Cherry wood one with orange epoxy are a couple favourites.
Where do you see you work going in the future?
I recently bought a bigger lathe: a Laguna 1836, and want to
make bigger pieces than what I made on a prior Laguna 1216
lathe. I want to improve the finish of my pieces and add more
artistic flourishes.

Laburnum is widely
planted as an ornamen
tal tree in gardens. It is a
small tree growing only
to 30 feet tall and 8 -10
inches in diameter. It
is inconspicuous most
of the year except for
the Spring, when it has
masses of small yellow
flowers—hence the com
mon name.
The species is native to Europe, where there are two in
the genus: Laburnum anagyroides and Laburnum alpi
num. These were crossed bred to give us the ornamen
tal cultivar.
Laburnum is hard (Janka
Hardness 2,000 lb). Despite this
the wood is easy to work and
is excellent for turning. The
sapwood is light yellow and
the heartwood is orange brown
to dark brown in mature trees.
This contrast between the sap
wood and heartwood can be used for interesting effect.
Because of its hardness and darkness, the heartwood
has often been used as a Ebony substitute. The wood
is considered non-perishable and is excellent for tool
handles and small pieces.
Laburnum is toxic with all parts containing the com
pound Cytisine, especially the seed pods. The seed
pods are long and slender resembling bean pods mak
ing them dangerously attractive to children. Cytisine
has the same action as Nicotine and has a long history
of being used as a Nicotine replacement. The leaves
were smoked by solders as a tobacco substitute during
WW2. In North America it is marketed as “Cravy” and
is an agent approved by Health Canada to assist with
stopping smoking.
Ingestion can cause nausea and indigestion, but serious
toxicity is rare depending on amount ingested. Caution
should be exercised when turning and working with
Laburnum which can potentially lead to exposure.

Spring Intro to
Spindle Turning Class
by Ed Pretty
On May 9 & 10 the GVWG held a hands-on session on spindle
turning techniques. There were 6 students with varying levels
of turning skill, Brian Lunt as assistant and Ed Pretty as lead
instructor. All students were at least comfortable with turning
bowls but although some had tried spindle turning, none felt
they were comfortable with spindle techniques. The learning
objectives were to be able to create the three basic shapes
found in spindle turning: straight or curved barrel shapes,
beads and coves. As always seems to be the case, the number
one expectation of most students was to gain confidence with
the skew.
We started the first day with learning various ways to use the
spindle roughing gouge, the last one akin to using a skew. The
natural step after that was using a skew to do straight planing
cuts. In general, confidence built fairly quickly so we explored
long radius barrel and cove shapes. Although these weren’t
prescribed objectives, everyone gave them a try with varying
degrees of success. Though the skills varied, confidence with
the skew was evident in all students.
On the second day we concentrated on creating beads and
coves with a spindle gouge. Both techniques require combin
ing three motions together in harmony so, understandably,
there was quite a bit of frustration at the start. Nevertheless,
after quite a bit of practice, most students were able to get
the combination consistently and were able to produce quite
uniform shapes with crisp edges.
We ended the day with a demonstration and discussion on
producing repetitive pieces using a story board.
I always look forward to these sessions. I find that confidence
in spindle techniques broadens a turner’s skill, typically pro
viding greater control when turning bowls.
